evidence.quote: When the 11 ships of the First Fleet arrived in Australia from England in 1788, they brought not only convicts, soldiers, plants and animals from Britain to the new colony of New South Wales, but also the colony’s first printing press and first books. evidence.quote: In 1821 a catalogue of books in the personal libraries belonging to private citizens in the colony was compiled. From these, a number of libraries began to emerge. evidence.quote: Traditionally, scholars have studied literature by intensively looking at individual written texts or perhaps comparing a few such texts. However, today, with the use of advanced computer technology, some researchers are aggregating and analysing massive quantities of information including words from thousands of texts. Franco Moretti, founder of the Literary Lab at Stanford University in the USA, is one such researcher. He tackles literary problems by scientific means: hypothesis-testing, computational modelling and quantitative analysis. He advocates understanding literature not by studying individual texts, but by applying rigorous scientific methods to study an enormous number of texts collectively. Only in that way, Moretti argues, can you identify broad literary patterns and currents. A good example of this approach can be found in the work of a team of researchers at Dartmouth College in the USA, led by Professor Daniel Rockmore. The Dartmouth group set out to study the evolution of the literary styles of authors writing in English between the 16th and the 20th centuries, looking at literary trends across many works. The research used data from 7,733 digitised books written by 537 authors available from the Project Gutenberg library.

14.explanation: Phân tích số lượng văn bản lớn giúp tìm xu hướng chung.

evidence.quote: The Dartmouth researchers focused on the usage of ‘content-free’ words like prepositions (e.g. ‘of’, ‘in’, ‘to’), conjunctions (e.g. ‘and’, ‘but’), and articles (e.g. ‘the’, ‘a’, ‘an’) which, Professor Rockmore explained, are useful for stylistic analysis because they do not convey meaning. While content words can yield data about subject matter, content-free words can provide data for the analysis of literary style. Professor Rockmore says that content-free words form the ‘glue’ of language: they carry little or no meaning on their own but form the bridge between words that do convey meaning and thus provide useful stylistic fingerprints for literary characteristics.

15.explanation: Từ không mang nội dung được chọn để phân tích phong cách.

evidence.quote: The Dartmouth researchers found that the writing of authors in the 18th and 19th centuries was stylistically similar, and was strongly affected by the writing of their predecessors from previous centuries. Therefore 18th- and 19th-century authors displayed a remarkably similar choice of words, phrasing, meaning and grammar. This resulted in significant stylistic stability, with styles remaining relatively unchanged for extensive periods. However, authors writing in the 20th century were most affected by other 20th-century writers. In other words, the past seems to be exerting a diminishing stylistic influence on the present. If one believes that writing style is significantly related to popular speech, then the diminishing importance of the past might be traced to the speed with which spoken communication is changing today. According to Professor Rockmore, another reason for this may be that because of the huge number of new books now coming on the market each year, people devote less of their reading time to the ‘classics’ and are thus less affected by them.

16.explanation: Nguồn sách mới lớn làm đọc kinh điển ít và giảm ảnh hưởng quá khứ.

evidence.quote: The prize-winning American novelist Lionel Shriver agrees that her own writing style has not been very much affected by older literary works, and suggests that this is likely to apply to other modern writers as well. She confesses that while she devoured classics in her teens and 20s, she now reads contemporary fiction almost exclusively. With all the other things she does, like writing book reviews, she doesn’t often get around to the classics. She says, ‘I’ve discovered that I don’t have the patience any longer – for the long philosophical digressions, for example. I bet I’m not alone in this reduced tolerance for the stylistic traditions of the past.’

evidence.quote: While digital literary analysis has been hailed by some scholars as an opportunity to revitalise the field of literary studies, others remain unconvinced. Dartmouth English professor Aden Evens fears that the new methods of analysis provided by digitisation will appeal to different people, including university administrators who to some extent control or at least help decide on the funding of academic research. Evens continues, ‘What I am worried about is that we are asked to set aside what most distinguishes the humanities – our ability to perform critiques of ambiguity – and instead we are being asked to supplant it with a view of knowledge that promotes certainty, statistical or numerical style analyses, absolute and clear distinctions.’

evidence.quote: Other scholars feel that quantitative methodologies will never replace the more usual ways of studying literary texts. In interpreting what the numbers mean, a literary scholar has to bring in all the knowledge of literature and authors that is applied in customary literary studies. Computer-based interpretation of texts, however, can provide opportunities to ask new questions about literature. According to James Hughes, a member of the Dartmouth team, researchers using computational tools do not claim to employ the ‘best’ approach to literature. ‘The point is really,’ writes Hughes, ‘that traditional analyses that take into account the intangible or unquantifiable factors can benefit from the addition of quantitative evidence.’

evidence.quote: Many linguists predict that at least half the world's 6,000 or so languages will be dead or dying by the year 2050. Languages are becoming extinct at twice the rate of endangered mammals and four times the rate of endangered birds. If this trend continues, the world of the future could be dominated by a dozen or fewer languages. Michael Krauss, director of the Alaska Native Language Center, suggests that as many as 90 per cent of languages could be dying or extinct by 2100. According to Krauss, 20 to 40 per cent of languages are already declining, and only 5 to 10 per cent are 'safe' in the sense of being widely spoken or having official status. If people 'become wise and turn it around', Krauss says, the number of dead or dying languages could perhaps be 50 per cent by 2100.

evidence.quote: The definition of a healthy language is one that acquires new speakers. No matter how many adults use the language, if it isn't passed to the next generation, its future as a living language is in jeopardy. A language may continue to exist for a long time as a second or ceremonial language, but it is on the way out as soon as children stop learning it. Although language extinction is sad for the people involved, why should the rest of us care? Replacing a minor language with a more widespread one may even seem like a good thing, allowing people to communicate with each other more easily. But it isn't. Dr Clayton noted exactly what the birds had hidden and where, and then put the birds in a cage. She later returned the birds to the area where they had hidden the food, in some cases after four hours and in other cases after five days. evidence.quote: In the primitive insect societies, conflict and competition lead to the emergence of a single female, the queen, which physically dominates the rest of the adult members of the colony. In the more advanced insect societies, particularly those in which strong differences between the queen and worker castes exist, the queen also exercises control over the workers, but usually in a more subtle manner, without obvious aggression. This evolutionary change, from what might be regarded as rough dominance to the more refined methods of queen control, is one of the clear-cut adaptations that extend across the social insects as a whole, and one worth tracing in some detail.

evidence.quote: Aggression and dominance were first recorded by the Swiss scientist Pierre Huber (1802) In his pioneering study of bumblebees. He saw that when a queen lays her eggs, some of the workers try to steal and eat them, but the queen usually repels these Intruders with great anger. Similar findings have been reported by a long line of subsequent investigators. The Austrian Eduard Hoffer (1882-1883) discovered that: 'punishment is almost always administered with the legs and mandibles, and the guilty individual never even attempts to defend herself, all her efforts being directed toward making the quickest possible escape. The punishment is sometimes so rough that the poor creature is seriously wounded or even killed.' Once egg stealing has been repelled for a few hours, the attempts by the workers become less and less frequent, and finally cease altogether; and these same little Insects which previously tried 'their very best to get rid of the newly-laid eggs, now become attentive guardians and nurses of their embryo brothers and sisters; they keep them warm and tenderly provide them with nourishment continuously thereafter.'

evidence.quote: Egg stealing puzzled the early observers; it seemed to them such strange behaviour, as if the bumblebees were heading for race suicide. Huber offered a surprisingly modern hypothesis. He stated: ‘The bumblebees are the largest insects that feed on honey; and if their number trebled or quadrupled, other insects would not find any nourishment, and perhaps their species would be wiped out.' Perez (1899) viewed egg eating as simply evidence of selfish behaviour on the part of the workers, and therefore an Imperfection in the social order. But there is a more straightforward explanation of the phenomenon: Lindhard (1912) observed an Instance In which a queen of the species Bombus lapidaries extracted the egg of a rival worker and fed it to a queen larva. Also noting that very few, if any, worker-laid eggs ever survive, he hypothesized that the objects are not meant to develop but instead provide food for prospective queens. If there is any truth in this conclusion, It Is consistent with the general occurrence of unfertilized eggs laid by workers of related insect species.

evidence.quote: The existence of a similar dominance system in the paper wasp, Polistes gallicus, was suggested by Heldmann (1936), who found that when two or more females start a nest together, one comes to function as the main egg layer, and therefore queen, while the others take up the role of workers. The queen feeds more on the eggs laid by the workers than the reverse, thus exercising a form of reproductive dominance. However, the relationship among the adult members of the wasp colony is somewhat more elaborate in form than that in bumblebee colonies. Instead of simple dictatorship by the queen, there exists in most cases a series of ranks, involving a principal egg layer, the queen, and the remainder of the associated females, called auxiliaries. The relative intensities of egg laying, food gathering, and comb building are graded accordingly. Dominant individuals receive more food whenever food is exchanged, they lay more eggs, and they contribute less work. They establish and maintain their rank by a series of frequently repeated aggressive encounters.

17.explanation: Xếp hạng gắn với được ăn nhiều, đẻ nhiều và làm ít.

evidence.quote: At their lowest intensity these encounters are simply a matter of posture; the dominant individual rises on its legs to a level higher than the subordinate, while the subordinate crouches and lowers its antennae. At higher intensities leg biting occurs, and at highest intensity the wasps attempt to sting each other. The severest conflicts occur between wasps of nearly equal rank, and during the early days of the association when the nest is first being constructed. As time passes, the wasps fit more easily into their roles, and aggressive exchanges become more subdued, less frequent, and eventually purely postural in nature. When the first adult workers emerge from the pupa*, during later stages of colony development, their relations to the founders of the colony are invariably subordinate and non-violent. The workers also form a hierarchy among themselves; those that emerge early tend to dominate their younger nestmates. If the head female is removed, the next highest auxiliaries intensify their hostility to each other until one of their number becomes definitely dominant; then the exchanges subside to the previous low level.

evidence.quote: Throughout history, clothing has served many social purposes. One of the most fundamental aspects of dress in most societies is the custom that the dress of men and women should be different. These differences reflect culturally-determined views of the social roles appropriate to each gender. What is considered appropriate may differ markedly from one place to another. For many centuries in Western Europe, for example, trousers were generally designated as male dress. Clothing may also serve to mark age associated changes. Thus throughout the 19th century, younger girls in Western Europe wore shorter skirts than their adolescent sisters. What a person wears may also convey other information about the wearer, as when a wedding ring worn on a specific finger signifies that he or she is in a marital relationship. Similarly, it was once customary in Europe for married women to cover their hair, while young unmarried women were permitted to go without head covering.

The nature of this political structure — an absolute monarchy — was mirrored in the attitude to clothing. Other aspects of social organization may be manifest in dress. Special clothing may also be involved in ceremonies which serve to strengthen the community, as when the inhabitants of a town dress in historic costume to celebrate the anniversary of the founding of the town. evidence.quote: Dress, therefore, discloses the social stratification of society, revealing whether it has rigid delineations of social and economic class or is a relatively classless society. For example, the political leaders in the African Ashanti tribe wore distinctive dress marking their special social position. No subject was allowed to wear the same fabric pattern as the king. The nature of this political structure — an absolute monarchy — was mirrored in the attitude to clothing. Other aspects of social organization may be manifest in dress. The garments worn by those leading a religious service may or may not distinguish them from the worshippers, again reflecting the way that religion is seen by members of that community.

evidence.quote: As well as differentiating between social groups, clothing also serves other purposes. Sociologists speak of rites of passage, marking the passage of the individual from one status to another. Special clothing may also be involved in ceremonies which serve to strengthen the community, as when the inhabitants of a town dress in historic costume to celebrate the anniversary of the founding of the town. Designated forms of dress are frequently an important part of the ceremonies associated with such rites. Clothing is also a means of enhancing the attractiveness of individuals. evidence.quote: The evidence comes from the San Juan mountains of southwest Colorado, downwind of Arizona and New Mexico. There Jason Neff, a geochemist from the University of Colorado, has been analyzing sediments, the sand, stones and mud, laid down over the past 5000 years. Atmospheric dust was minimal throughout those five millennia until the mid-19th century, he says, but then, 'from about 1860 to 1900, dust deposition rates shot up.'

evidence.quote: This is surprising because usually dry means dusty, and the American West has almost always been dry-often drier than today. evidence.quote: This was not the case with the European settlers once they brought their cows. evidence.quote: In the Great Plains to the east and north, bison roamed in vast herds. Their regular grazing had created tough grass, while the herds manured the soil. In the Southwest, the land had few defenses against a sudden invasion of millions of livestock, whose teeth stripped the grass and whose hooves punctured the hard crust of desert soils that protected them from the wind. The invasion was sudden, funded by a bubble of speculative investment, much of it from Britain. The money went into railroads, and herds of cattle and sheep that rode the rails to the wide open pastures. By 1900, when sedimentation rates peaked, there were 20 million cattle and 25 million sheep in the West.

evidence.quote: One of the biggest ranches was owned by the Aztec Land and Cattle Company, which owned a million acres of land by 1884. Each acre had cost the company a mere 50 cents, and like many other speculators, it was only interested in quick profits and had little incentive to protect the soils from overgrazing. By the time Aztec sold the ranch in 1901, it was barren, with cattle carcasses scattered across the exhausted land. Such was the damage to the grasslands that even now few of the pastures have recovered. The parched and exposed soil simply blew away. The 1862 Homestead Act was passed in order to encourage the populating of the West. Any family willing to make the journey was entitled to claim 160 acres and farm it.
